title: When and why PINNs fail to train: A neural tangent kernel perspective
authors_full: Sifan Wang, Xinling Yu, Paris Perdikaris
affiliations: Graduate Group in Applied Mathematics and Computational Science, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA (Wang, Yu); Department of Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA (Perdikaris)
subdomain: Training dynamics of PINNs via the neural tangent kernel (NTK): GP/NTK convergence theory, spectral bias, inter-term convergence-rate discrepancy, and NTK-based adaptive loss weighting
industry_context: No industry or company named; academic theory paper (University of Pennsylvania, Predictive Intelligence Lab). Funding: US DOE Advanced Scientific Computing Research de-sc0019116 and AFOSR FA9550-20-1-0060.
physics_enforced_exact: General well-posed PDE L[u](x) = f(x), x in Omega, with u(x) = g(x) on the boundary (eqs. 3.1-3.2), L a differential operator; initial condition treated as a special type of Dirichlet condition. Concrete cases: 1D Poisson u_xx(x) = f(x) on (0,1), u = 0 at x = 0,1, with fabricated solutions u(x) = sin(pi*x) (f = -pi^2 sin(pi*x)) and u(x) = sin(4*pi*x) (f = -16*pi^2 sin(4*pi*x)); 1D wave equation u_tt(x,t) - 4*u_xx(x,t) = 0 on (0,1)x(0,1), u(0,t) = u(1,t) = 0, u(x,0) = sin(pi*x) + 1/2 sin(4*pi*x), u_t(x,0) = 0, exact solution u = sin(pi*x)cos(2*pi*t) + 1/2 sin(4*pi*x)cos(8*pi*t) (d'Alembert).
pde_type: multiple (elliptic 1D Poisson + hyperbolic 1D wave; theory stated for any differential operator L)
dimensionality: 1D (Poisson on unit interval) and 1D+time (wave on (0,1)x(0,1)); theory formulated for general d-dimensional PDEs
nonlinearity: linear (both experimental PDEs are linear; GP-convergence proof, Theorem 4.1, is for linear operators and Remark 4.2 extends it to any linear differential operator; the NTK evolution lemma holds for any L, and for general nonlinear PDEs the NTK may not remain fixed during training)
bcs_ic_handled: Dirichlet boundary data g and source f enter as supervised least-squares targets; for the wave equation the temporal coordinate t is treated as an additional spatial coordinate so the initial displacement u(x,0) is folded into g on the boundary of the (x,t) domain, and the initial velocity u_t(x,0) = 0 is imposed as a separate least-squares term; collocation points in the domain enforce the PDE residual.
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty (standard composite PINN loss; the paper's contribution is the NTK analysis of this soft-constraint training dynamics and a re-weighting of the soft penalties, not a new constraint mechanism)
enforcement_details: Residual r(x,theta) := L[u(x,theta)] - f(x) formed by automatic differentiation of the network output. Loss L(theta) = L_b(theta) + L_r(theta) with L_b = 1/2 sum |u(x_b,theta) - g(x_b)|^2, L_r = 1/2 sum |r(x_r,theta)|^2. Key construct: the NTK of a PINN is the block matrix K(t) = [[K_uu, K_ur],[K_ru, K_rr]] whose entries are parameter-space inner products of Jacobians, e.g. (K_uu)_ij = <du(x_i)/dtheta, du(x_j)/dtheta>, (K_rr)_ij = <dL(x_i)/dtheta, dL(x_j)/dtheta>; under gradient flow d[u; Lu]/dt = -K(t) [u - g; Lu - f] (Lemma 3.1), which holds for ANY differential operator and ANY network architecture (Remark 3.4). Training-error components decay as exp(-lambda_i t) in the eigenbasis of K(0), so the NTK spectrum at initialization governs convergence of each loss component.
network_architecture: Fully-connected MLP in NTK parameterization (eq. 2.3: f(x,theta) = 1/sqrt(N) W^(1) sigma(W^(0)x + b^(0)) + b^(1)), i.i.d. N(0,1) initialization: 1 hidden layer of width 10/100/500 for NTK convergence tests (Sec. 7.1), 1 hidden layer of width 100 for the Poisson adaptive-weight tests (Sec. 7.2), and 5 hidden layers x 500 neurons for the 1D wave equation (Sec. 7.3, Glorot initialization). Theory/proofs are restricted to one-hidden-layer networks; multi-layer behavior is observed numerically and conjectured.
activation_function: hyperbolic tangent (tanh) in all experiments; theory assumes smooth sigma with bounded derivatives up to 4th order ('satisfied by most of the activation functions commonly used for PINNs such as sigmoids, hyperbolic tangents, sine functions, etc.')
input_representation: spatial coordinate x in R^d (Poisson); spatio-temporal input x = (x,t) with time treated as an additional spatial coordinate (wave equation); no extra features
output_representation: scalar latent solution field u(x,theta); its autodiff images Lu(x,theta) (e.g. u_xx for Poisson, u_tt - 4u_xx for the wave equation) and u_t serve as residual/initial-condition outputs
loss_terms: Generic (eqs. 3.4-3.6, 6.2): L(theta) = L_b(theta) + L_r(theta) = lambda_b/(2*N_b) * sum_{i=1}^{N_b} |u(x_b^i,theta) - g(x_b^i)|^2 + lambda_r/(2*N_r) * sum_{i=1}^{N_r} |r(x_r^i,theta)|^2, with r = L[u] - f. Wave equation (eqs. 7.10-7.11): L(theta) = L_b + L_u + L_r = lambda_b/(2*N_w) sum |u(x_g,theta) - g|² + lambda_u/(2*N_u) sum |u_t(x_u,theta)|^2 (initial-velocity condition) + lambda_r/(2*N_r) sum |Lu(x_r,theta)|^2, L = d_tt - 4*d_xx, N_w = N_u = N_r = 300.
loss_weighting: adaptive NTK-based (Algorithm 1): initialize lambda_b = lambda_r = 1; at each iteration (or a user-specified frequency, e.g. every 10 steps) set lambda_b = Tr(K(n))/Tr(K_uu(n)) and lambda_r = Tr(K(n))/Tr(K_rr(n)), using kernel traces instead of full eigendecompositions to save compute; wave-equation variant uses generalized trace-ratio rules (eqs. 7.13-7.15) updated every 1,000 iterations. Observed: lambda_b and lambda_u rise rapidly then stay fixed while lambda_r stays near 1. Alternative stability knob discussed: batch size <-> learning rate, with max stable lr <= 2/lambda_max(K̄(t)).
sampling_strategy: Poisson: N_b = N_r = 100 boundary/residual points uniformly spaced on the unit interval (full-batch). Wave equation: N_w = N_u = N_r = 300 points uniformly sampled in the computational domain at each gradient-descent iteration (mini-batch).
optimizer_schedule: NTK convergence and Poisson experiments: standard full-batch gradient descent, learning rate 1e-5, for 10,000 iterations (Sec. 7.1) and 40,000 iterations (Sec. 7.2); stability requires lr <= 2/lambda_max(K̄(t)). Wave equation: Adam with default settings for 80,000 iterations.
training_compute: not stated (no hardware or wall-clock training times reported)
data_regime: physics-only (no solution data): source f and boundary/initial data g come from manufactured exact solutions; N_b = N_r = 100 collocation/boundary points (Poisson); N_w = N_u = N_r = 300 (wave equation)
datasets_used: 1D Poisson equation on (0,1) with u = sin(pi*x) (NTK convergence study) and u = sin(4*pi*x) (adaptive-weight study); 1D wave equation u_tt - 4u_xx = 0 on (0,1)^2 with manufactured solution u = sin(pi*x)cos(2*pi*t) + 1/2 sin(4*pi*x)cos(8*pi*t)
baselines_compared: standard PINNs (Raissi et al. 2019) with equal weights lambda_b = lambda_r = 1 vs. the proposed NTK-adaptively weighted PINN (Algorithm 1); additionally a fixed-weight sensitivity sweep lambda_b in [1,500]
evaluation_metrics: relative L2 error of predicted solution vs. exact solution; point-wise error; relative change of parameters ||theta(n)-theta(0)||/||theta(0)|| and of the NTK ||K(n)-K(0)||/||K(0)|| during training; NTK eigenvalue spectra (descending order); average convergence rate c = Tr(K)/n of a kernel matrix (Definition 5.1)
key_quantitative_results: - NTK constancy (Sec. 7.1, Figs. 2-3): 1-hidden-layer PINN (widths 10/100/500, tanh, lr 1e-5, 10,000 GD steps) on Poisson u=sin(pi*x): relative change of weights and of the NTK tends to zero as width grows; eigenvalues of K at n=0 and n=10,000 barely change (width 500); same qualitative behavior with 3 hidden layers. - Poisson u=sin(4*pi*x), width 100, 40,000 GD steps, lr 1e-5 (Sec. 7.2): standard PINN rel. L2 = 2.40e-01; NTK-adaptive weights (computed lambda_b ~ 100, lambda_r = 1) rel. L2 = 1.63e-03, improving accuracy by about two orders of magnitude. - 1D wave equation, 5x500 MLP, Adam, 80,000 iterations (Sec. 7.3): standard PINN rel. L2 = 4.518e-01 ('above 40%'); Algorithm 1 with weights updated every 1,000 iterations rel. L2 = 1.728e-03. - Spectral structure (Sec. 5, Fig. 1): NTK eigenvalues of PINNs decay rapidly and most are near zero (spectral bias), and K_rr dominates K_uu so the PDE residual converges much faster than the boundary conditions; on the wave problem K_u and K_u_t dominate K_r. - Weight sweep (Fig. 5): averaging rel. L2 over 10 independent trials with lambda_b in [1,500], error drops to a local minimum near lambda_b ~ 100 (matching the NTK-suggested value) then oscillates; very large lambda_b gives large standard deviation due to imaginary eigenvalues of the indefinite weighted kernel.
errors_reported: rel. L2 = 2.40e-01 (Poisson sin(4*pi*x), standard PINN, 1x100 MLP, 40k GD iters) vs rel. L2 = 1.63e-03 (same case, adaptive lambda_b = 100, lambda_r = 1); rel. L2 = 4.518e-01 (1D wave, standard PINN, 5x500 MLP, Adam 80k iters) vs rel. L2 = 1.728e-03 (same case, Algorithm 1)
speedup_claims: No speedup claims; the benefit is trainability and accuracy (~100x error reduction). The extra cost of computing NTK traces (weights updated every 1,000 iterations in the wave case) is described as negligible compared to a standard PINNs approach.
ablations: (i) Width study 10/100/500 with 1 hidden layer (and 3 hidden layers): relative parameter/NTK change decreases toward zero as width grows, supporting NTK convergence and constancy; (ii) eigenvalue snapshot of K at initialization vs. n = 10,000 (width 500): all eigenvalues barely change; (iii) fixed-weight sweep lambda_b in [1,500], 10 independent trials, averaged: optimum near lambda_b ~ 100 agrees with the NTK trace-based suggestion, while very large lambda_b destabilizes training (imaginary eigenvalues of indefinite K̄); (iv) eigenvalue tracking of K̄ (and of K_u, K_u_t, K_r) at n = 0, 10,000, 40,000, 80,000 during wave-equation training: eigenvalues move 'outward' early then stay almost static, and the adaptive weights (Fig. 8a) rise quickly then remain fixed, showing Algorithm 1 is stable.
stated_limitations: Authors state (Sec. 8, Discussion): the proposed NTK theory is a first step with many open questions - whether it extends to fully-connected networks with multiple hidden layers, nonlinear equations, and other architectures (convolutional, residual networks); PINNs perform much better on inverse than forward problems and the current theory does not analyze inverse problems; training dynamics under momentum (e.g. Adam) and the NTK evolution under momentum are not analyzed; 'despite some improvements... assigning weights to the loss function... cannot change the distribution of eigenvalues of the NTK and thus, cannot directly resolve spectral bias'; assigning weights may result in indefinite kernels with imaginary eigenvalues and unstable training processes. Also (Sec. 6): for general nonlinear PDEs the NTK of PINNs may not remain fixed during training; and (Sec. 4) 'from the authors' experience, the NTK of PINNs is always degenerate', so infinite-width kernel-regression predictions may not be performable in practice. Proofs are for one-hidden-layer networks; multi-hidden-layer constancy is only conjectured from numerics (Sec. 7.1).
failure_modes: Core subject of the paper: (1) PINNs with fully-connected architectures often fail to achieve stable training and accurate predictions when the PDE solution contains high-frequency or multi-scale features (Sec. 1, citing Wang et al. arXiv:2001.04536 who attribute it to stiffness in gradient flow); (2) spectral bias - NTK eigenvalues decay rapidly and most are near zero, so high-frequency components of the target function converge extremely slowly (Sec. 5); (3) a remarkable discrepancy in convergence rates among loss components: eigenvalues of K_rr are much greater than K_uu, so the PDE residual converges much faster than the boundary conditions, identified as 'one of the key fundamental reasons behind why PINNs can often fail to train'; (4) very large loss weights make the weighted kernel K̄ indefinite with imaginary eigenvalues, causing unstable training (Sec. 7.2); (5) for general nonlinear PDEs the NTK may not stay fixed during training (Sec. 6).
reproducibility: Public code and data: https://github.com/PredictiveIntelligenceLab/PINNsNTK ('The data and code accompanying this manuscript are publicly available'); 'all results presented in this section can be reproduced using our publicly available code'. No random seeds or hardware specs stated. DeepXDE library referenced [43]. Funding: DOE de-sc0019116, AFOSR FA9550-20-1-0060.
quotable_finding: We believe that such a discrepancy between K_uu and K_rr is one of the key fundamental reasons behind why PINNs can often fail to train and yield accurate predictions. (p. 8)
relevance_rqs: RQ2 (components): supplies the NTK-based adaptive loss-weighting mechanism (Algorithm 1) as a canonical loss-balancing component; RQ3 (physics+mechanism): explains mechanically WHY soft-penalty multi-term physics losses train unevenly (NTK spectrum at initialization; K_rr >> K_uu; error components decay as exp(-lambda_i*t)) and how trace-based reweighting rebalances convergence rates; RQ4 (reviews+reliability): foundational reference for PINN trainability/failure diagnosis (spectral bias, high-frequency solutions, unstable weighting).
manuscript_section: S4 methods (loss-weighting strategies and NTK-based adaptive weights; enforcement-mechanism analysis of soft penalties); T1/T2 methods-and-training tables; F2/F4 figures on failure modes and weighting mechanisms; also feeds the survey's reliability discussion (RQ4).
cross_paper_links: builds-on PINN-A01 (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis 2019, cited as [39] - 'Following the original work of Raissi et al. [39]'); compares-to/extends Wang, Teng, Perdikaris arXiv:2001.04536 (gradient pathologies / learning-rate annealing, cited [28]): the NTK weighting gives the theoretical justification that the empirical scheme lacked; builds on Jacot et al. 2018 NTK [33], Rahaman et al. 2019 spectral bias [29], Xu et al. frequency principle [41]; cites DeepONet (Lu, Jin, Karniadakis, arXiv:1910.03193 [23]) only in the introductory application list
notes_caveats: Analyzed PDF is the arXiv v1 preprint (arXiv:2007.14527v1, dated 28 Jul 2020, 'A PREPRINT'); the JCP 2022 version is the same work, so page numbers cited here refer to the preprint pagination. Proofs (Theorems 4.1/4.3/4.4) are restricted to one-hidden-layer networks under strong assumptions (bounded parameters, infinitesimally small learning rate, smooth activation with bounded derivatives up to 4th order) and to linear PDEs for the GP correspondence; multi-layer and nonlinear behavior is conjectured/observed numerically only. Experiments are exclusively 1D manufactured-solution toy cases (Poisson, wave) - no 2D/3D, no real data, no comparison to numerical PDE solvers. The 'always degenerate' NTK claim is empirical (authors' experience). In the PDF, subscripts of the wave-equation loss terms and updating rules (eqs. 7.11, 7.13-7.15) are partially ambiguous in rendering; the three-term structure and trace-ratio updating are unambiguous. Despite the toy scope, ~1880 citations reflect its role as the canonical NTK-based explanation of PINN training failure and the origin of NTK-guided loss weighting.
